title: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
summary: Use the shell as a working tool: files and permissions, scripts, text tools (grep, sed, awk), job control, ssh and tmux, built on how bash runs commands: fork and exec, expansion, redirection, pipes and exit statuses.
outcomes: Navigate the filesystem, read ls -l permissions and set them with chmod
Explain how bash finds, forks and execs a command and predict its arguments after expansion and quoting
Write scripts with tests, loops and functions that survive spaces in names and fail loudly
Explain redirection and pipes with the fd table, and build text pipelines with grep, regex, sed and awk
Control jobs and signals, clean up with trap, configure startup files, and work remotely with ssh and tmux

lessons.title: Files, paths and permissions: finding your way around

blocks.md: Before looking at how the shell runs commands, you need to move around. Unix-like systems such as Linux and macOS keep every file in **one tree**. Its top is the **root directory**, written `/`, and every other directory hangs below it: `/home`, `/etc`, `/home/ana/proj`. A **path** names a place in the tree by listing directory names joined with slashes. (Windows instead has one root per disk, such as `C:`; this course assumes Linux or macOS.)

A path that starts with `/` is **absolute**: it is read from the root, so it means the same thing wherever you are. Any other path is **relative**: it is read from your **current working directory**, the directory a process is in. `pwd` (print working directory) shows it and `cd` (change directory) changes it. Every directory contains two special names: `.` is the directory itself and `..` is its parent. The shell also turns a leading `~` into your **home directory**, the place your shell starts in, such as `/home/ana` (lesson 3 shows when this happens).

blocks.title: Moving around one tree with cd

scenes.caption: You start in your home directory, `/home/ana`. `pwd` prints that absolute path: the directory names on the way down from the root `/`.
`cd proj/src` is relative: it starts at the current directory and walks down two levels. `pwd` now prints `/home/ana/proj/src`.
`cd ../..` climbs to the parent twice, from src to proj and then to ana. Each `..` is one level up.
`cd /etc` is absolute, so it starts at the root wherever you are. `ls` here would list `hosts`.
`cd ~/proj` works from anywhere: the shell replaces `~` with `/home/ana` before cd runs, so cd receives an absolute path.

blocks.md:
A handful of commands do most of the daily work:

- `ls` lists a directory; `ls -a` also shows names that start with a dot, which are hidden by default (configuration files such as `.bashrc` use this)
- `mkdir -p a/b` makes a directory, creating missing parents
- `cp src dst` copies; `cp -r` copies a directory and everything in it (r for recursive)
- `mv old new` moves or renames
- `rm file` removes a file; `rm -r dir` removes a whole tree
- `echo words` prints its arguments, and `cat f` prints a whole file
- `less f` shows a file one screen at a time (q quits); `head -n 5 f` and `tail -n 5 f` show its first or last lines, and `tail -f log` keeps printing lines as they are added
- `wc -l f` counts the lines in a file

`rm` unlinks the names immediately. There is no trash folder to restore from.

blocks.code:
$ mkdir -p proj/src
$ touch proj/README proj/.env proj/src/main.c
$ ls proj
README  src
$ ls -a proj
.       ..      .env    README  src
$ cp -r proj proj-copy
$ mv proj-copy proj-old
$ ls
proj            proj-old
$ rm -r proj-old
$ ls
proj
blocks.caption: A real bash session in an empty folder. `touch` creates empty files. `ls` hides `.env` until you add `-a`, and `.` and `..` appear in every directory.

blocks.md: `ls -l` (long format) prints one line per file. The POSIX standard fixes the fields in order: the file **mode**, the number of links (names that refer to this same file), the owner, the group, the size in bytes, the time of the last modification, and the name. The mode is ten characters: a type (`-` regular file, `d` directory, `l` symbolic link), then three groups of `rwx` for the file's **owner** (also called the user), its **group**, and **others**. A letter means the permission is granted and `-` means it is not. Some systems add an eleventh character: POSIX reserves it for an extra access control method, such as an access control list shown as `+`, and macOS also prints `@` for a file with extended attributes.

blocks.title: Nine permission bits become three octal digits

scenes.caption: The mode of a script after `chmod 755`. The first character is the type (`-` regular file); then three groups of three for owner, group and others.
Each position has a fixed weight: read 4, write 2, execute 1. They are the bits of a 3-bit binary number, so one octal digit (0 to 7) holds one group.
Add the weights of the letters present. Owner rwx is 4+2+1 = 7; group r-x is 4+0+1 = 5; others r-x is 5. The mode is 755.
Now `rw-r-----`: owner 4+2 = 6, group 4, others 0, so 640. The owner reads and writes, the group only reads, everyone else gets nothing.
`chmod u+x` sets one bit, the owner's execute bit worth 1, so 640 becomes 740. `chmod 755` would instead set all nine bits at once.

blocks.md: The kernel uses exactly **one** of the three groups for each access. If you own the file, the owner bits decide; otherwise, if you belong to the file's group, the group bits decide; otherwise the others bits. The groups are not combined, so an owner whose own bits are `---` is refused even when everyone else may read.

blocks.code:
$ printf 'echo built\n' > build.sh
$ ls -l build.sh | cut -c1-10
-rw-r--r--
$ ./build.sh
bash: ./build.sh: Permission denied
$ echo $?
126
$ chmod u+x build.sh
$ ls -l build.sh | cut -c1-10
-rwxr--r--
$ ./build.sh
built
$ chmod 640 build.sh
$ ls -l build.sh | cut -c1-10
-rw-r-----
$ chmod 755 build.sh
$ ls -l build.sh | cut -c1-10
-rwxr-xr-x
blocks.caption: Real bash session on macOS (`cut -c1-10` keeps just the ten mode characters, and `>` writes printf's output into build.sh, as lesson 5 explains). A new file is not executable, so running it fails with status 126, the code you will meet in lesson 2.

blocks.md: `chmod` (change mode) has two styles. **Symbolic**: `u`, `g`, `o` or `a` (all), then `+`, `-` or `=`, then letters. `chmod u+x f` adds the owner's execute bit and `chmod go-w f` removes write from group and others, leaving every other bit alone. **Numeric**: one octal digit per class, so `chmod 640 f` sets all nine bits at once. Symbolic is safer for one change; numeric states the whole final mode. Only the file's owner (or the administrator, root) may change its mode.

For a **directory** the letters mean something slightly different. `r` lets you list the names inside it, `w` lets you create, delete and rename entries in it, and `x`, called **search** permission, lets you enter it with `cd` and reach anything inside it by path. You need `x` on every directory along a path. Deleting a file changes its directory, not the file, so it needs `w` on the directory.

Every flag in this course comes from a manual. Most programs print a short summary with `--help` (or `-h`), and `man cmd` opens the full **manual page**. Manual pages are grouped into numbered **sections**: 1 for commands, 2 for system calls (requests a program makes to the kernel), 5 for file formats and configuration files, 7 for overviews. So one name can have two pages: `man 1 chmod` is the command and `man 2 chmod` is the system call it uses. A name written like `fork(2)` in this course means the page in section 2.

`rm` and `mv` act at once and say nothing. `mv` onto an existing name silently replaces that file, and `rm -r` cannot be undone. Before deleting with a pattern, run `ls` with the same pattern to see what it matches, and add `-i` to make `rm` or `mv` ask first.

A mode is nine bits in three groups of rwx (owner, group, others), written as three octal digits with r = 4, w = 2, x = 1. On a file, x means run it; on a directory, x means enter it. Exactly one group applies to you.

blocks.question: A directory has mode 750 (`rwxr-x---`). You are not its owner but you are in its group. What can you do?
options: List, enter and create files in it
List it and enter it, but not create or delete files in it
Nothing, because only the owner has rwx
Enter it but not list it
blocks.explain: The group digit 5 is r-x: r lets you list the names and x lets you enter and reach files inside. Creating or deleting entries needs w on the directory, which the group lacks. Others (digit 0) get nothing at all.

blocks.question: You run `chmod 044 notes.txt` on a file you own, giving `----r--r--`, then `cat notes.txt` as yourself. What happens?
options: It prints the file, since everyone else can read it
It prints the file, because owners can always read their own files
chmod fails, because the owner must keep read permission
Permission denied, because only the owner bits apply to you
blocks.explain: The kernel picks one class: you own the file, so only the owner bits (`---`) count, and the group and others bits are ignored. A real run prints `cat: notes.txt: Permission denied`. You can still `chmod 644` it back, because changing the mode needs ownership, not read permission.

lessons.title: What happens when you press Enter: lookup, fork, exec, wait

blocks.md: A **shell** is an ordinary program (bash, zsh, sh) that reads a line of text, turns it into a command, asks the kernel to run it, and waits. A **terminal** is the window that shows text and sends your keystrokes; the shell is the program running inside it. Everything in this course is about bash, the shell on most Linux servers, and the POSIX rules it follows. POSIX (Portable Operating System Interface) is the IEEE standard that fixes how Unix-like shells and tools behave, so a script written to it runs the same on Linux, macOS and other Unix systems. Two keys save most typing: Tab completes a command or file name, and the Up arrow (or Ctrl-R to search) recalls earlier commands.

When you type `grep -n TODO main.c` and press Enter, four things happen in order:

1. **Split** the line into words: `grep`, `-n`, `TODO`, `main.c`.
2. **Expand** special syntax such as `$HOME` or `*.c` (lesson 3).
3. **Find** what the first word names: a function, a builtin, or a program file.
4. **Run** it: create a child process, load the program into it, wait for its **exit status**, a small integer where 0 means success.

A **builtin** is a command implemented inside bash itself, such as `cd` or `echo`, so running it starts no new program. Program files are found through **PATH**, a variable whose value is a list of directories separated by colons, such as `/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin`.

blocks.title: How bash resolves a command name

scenes.caption: The shell looks at the first word after expansion. Everything after it becomes the program's arguments.
A name with a slash, like `./build.sh` or `/usr/bin/env`, is used as a path directly. No search happens.
Otherwise bash checks, in this order, its shell functions and then its builtins. Both run inside the shell itself, with no new process.

Neither? Bash walks the directories in `PATH` left to right and runs the first executable file with that name. It remembers where it found each name (the `hash` builtin lists them), so the next lookup is fast.
No directory has it: bash prints an error and the status is 127. A file that exists but lacks the execute bit of lesson 1 gives 126 instead.

blocks.code:
type -a echo
# echo is a shell builtin
# echo is /bin/echo
type cd
# cd is a shell builtin
echo "$PATH"
# /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
blocks.caption: `type` tells you which branch a name takes. Output from bash on macOS; the PATH line is an example and yours will differ.

blocks.md: To run a program, bash uses two system calls. `fork()` creates a new process by duplicating the shell: same memory contents, same open files, same current directory. A process refers to its open files by **file descriptors**, small numbers such as 0, 1 and 2 (lesson 5 covers them). In that child, `execve()` replaces the copied shell with the new program; on success it never returns. The parent shell meanwhile calls `wait` to collect the child's exit status. Doing it in two steps is what lets the shell adjust the child (redirect its files, set variables) between fork and exec.

scenes.caption: Bash has parsed `ls -l` and found `/bin/ls` on PATH. It asks the kernel for a new process.
The child starts as an exact copy of bash, including its open file descriptors and working directory.
In the child, bash applies any redirections, then calls execve. The kernel loads `/bin/ls` over the copy. Open files survive the exec by default.
Meanwhile the parent blocks in wait. When ls finishes, the kernel hands its exit status to the parent, and bash stores it in `$?`.

blocks.prompt: Bash runs `(cd /usr)` (the parentheses run the command in a child shell), then `pwd`. You started in `/tmp`. What does `pwd` print?
blocks.reveal: **/tmp.** A child process has its own copy of the current directory, so changing it cannot affect the parent. This is exactly why `cd` must be a builtin: the Bash Reference Manual says cd, break, continue and exec *cannot be implemented outside of the shell because they directly manipulate the shell itself*. A `/usr/bin/cd` program would change its own directory and then exit.

blocks.md: The same copy rule explains variables. A plain assignment `x=1` creates a **shell variable** that lives only in the shell. `export x` marks it for the **environment**, the list of NAME=value strings handed to every child at exec. A prefix assignment like `GREETING=hi ./app` puts the variable in that one child's environment and leaves the shell unchanged. To run a file's commands inside the current shell instead of in a child, use `source file`, or its POSIX spelling `. file`.

A command runs in a **copy** of the shell. It inherits open files, the working directory and exported variables, and nothing it changes flows back. Only builtins and functions run inside the shell itself.

blocks.question: A script `setup.sh` contains `cd build` and `export MODE=dev`. You run it as `./setup.sh`, then type `pwd`. What do you see?
options: Your original directory, and MODE is unset in your shell
The build directory, because the script changed into it
The build directory, but MODE is unset because export only affects children
An error, because cd is a builtin and cannot run in a script
blocks.explain: `./setup.sh` runs in a child bash process. Its cd and export change only that child, which then exits. To apply them to your current shell you must run the file inside it with `source setup.sh` (or `. setup.sh`).

blocks.question: You type `deploy` and get `command not found` with status 127, yet `ls -l ~/bin/deploy` shows the file exists with mode `-rwxr-xr-x`. What is the most likely cause?
options: The file needs a .sh extension
Exit status 127 means the program crashed while starting
`~/bin` is not one of the directories in PATH
Bash only searches PATH for builtins
blocks.explain: Names without a slash are only looked up in the PATH directories. Add the directory to PATH or call it by path, `~/bin/deploy`. Extensions mean nothing to the kernel, and a crash would give a different status.

lessons.title: Expansion and quoting: why rm $f can delete the wrong files

blocks.md: Between reading your line and running it, bash rewrites the words. These rewrites are called **expansions**. They make the shell powerful (`*.log` becomes every log file) and they cause the most common shell bugs, because a single word you typed can turn into several arguments, or into zero.

The bash manual fixes the order:

1. **brace expansion**: `{a,b}.log` becomes `a.log b.log`
2. **tilde, parameter, arithmetic expansion and command substitution**, left to right: `~`, `$f`, `$((1+2))`, `$(date)`
3. **word splitting**: unquoted results of step 2 are split on whitespace (the characters in `IFS`, the internal field separator, which holds space, tab and newline by default)
4. **filename expansion** (globbing): unquoted words containing `*`, `?` or `[` are replaced by matching file names
5. **quote removal**: the quote characters you typed disappear

In step 2, the tilde `~` becomes your home directory. **Parameter expansion** replaces `$f` with the value of the variable f. **Arithmetic expansion** replaces `$((1+2))` with its result, 3. **Command substitution** runs the command inside `$(date)` and puts what it prints in its place, minus trailing newlines. In step 4, the star `*` matches any run of characters (even none), the question mark `?` matches exactly one character, and square brackets `[ab]` match one character from the set inside them; these patterns are called **globs**.

Only brace expansion, word splitting and filename expansion can turn one word into several. The exceptions are `"$@"` and `$*`, which both stand for the full list of arguments passed to the script or function and expand to one word per argument, and an unquoted expansion that is empty, which is removed.

blocks.code:
$ cat s
#!/usr/bin/env bash
printf '[%s] ' "$@"; echo
printf '[%s] ' "$*"; echo
printf '[%s] ' $@; echo
printf '[%s] ' $*; echo
$ ./s 'a b' c
[a b] [c]
[a b c]
[a] [b] [c]
[a] [b] [c]
blocks.caption: Real bash run with two arguments, `a b` and `c`. Quoted `"$@"` keeps them as two words; quoted `"$*"` joins them into one word with a space; unquoted, both forms are word-split again, so `a b` falls apart.

blocks.prompt: A directory holds three files: `my doc`, `a.md` and `b.md`. You run `f="my doc"` and then `rm $f *.md`. Which files does rm try to delete?
blocks.reveal: **Four**: `my`, `doc`, `a.md` and `b.md`. The variable expands to `my doc`, then word splitting cuts it at the space into two arguments. rm never sees the name `my doc`, and if files called `my` or `doc` existed, it would delete them. Writing `"$f"` keeps it as one word.

scenes.caption: Bash first splits the line into words using its grammar: three words in each version. The quotes in the second row are still there.
Parameter expansion replaces `$f` with its value, `my doc`. Still one word in both rows: expansion alone does not split.
Word splitting runs only on unquoted expansion results. The top row's value is cut at the space into `my` and `doc`; the quoted one is protected.
Filename expansion replaces the unquoted pattern `*.md` with matching names in sorted order. Final argument lists: rm gets 4 names on top, 3 below.

blocks.code:
f="my doc"
printf '[%s] ' rm $f *.md; echo
# [rm] [my] [doc] [a.md] [b.md]
printf '[%s] ' rm "$f" *.md; echo
# [rm] [my doc] [a.md] [b.md]
printf '[%s] ' *.csv; echo
# [*.csv]
blocks.caption: `printf '[%s] '` prints each argument in brackets, a handy way to see exactly what a command receives. Real bash output.

blocks.md: Two more rules from the last line above. A glob that matches nothing is left as the literal text `*.csv` by default, so a program may receive a pattern it did not expect. And glob characters that come out of a variable are still globbed if the variable is unquoted: with `x='*.md'`, `ls $x` lists files while `ls "$x"` looks for a file literally named `*.md`.

Quoting styles differ in what they keep active. **Single quotes** keep every character literal: no `$`, no globbing. **Double quotes** still allow `$var`, `$(cmd)` and `$((math))`, but block word splitting and globbing. For forwarding a script's arguments, use `"$@"`: inside double quotes it expands to each argument as its own word, spaces intact.

Do not test your quoting in zsh and assume bash agrees. zsh, the default interactive shell on macOS, does **not** word-split unquoted parameter expansions unless the `SH_WORD_SPLIT` option is set. Scripts that start with `#!/bin/bash` or `#!/bin/sh` (a first line naming the interpreter, the shebang of lesson 4) follow the splitting rules shown here.

File names with spaces or newlines also break pipelines that pass names as text. The robust pattern separates names with the NUL byte (the byte whose value is 0), which cannot appear in a file name: `find . -name '*.log' -print0 | xargs -0 rm`. **xargs** reads words from its input and passes them as arguments to the command after it, here `rm`. Here `-print0` ends each name with NUL and `xargs -0` splits only on NUL, so quotes, spaces and backslashes are taken literally.
Quote every expansion (`"$f"`, `"$(cmd)"`, `"$@"`) unless you specifically want splitting and globbing. Unquoted is the exception you choose, not the default.

blocks.question: A script runs `for f in $(ls *.txt); do wc -l $f; done` in a folder containing `notes.txt` and `q3 report.txt`. What happens?
options: It works: the glob keeps each file name intact
wc is called on `notes.txt`, `q3` and `report.txt`, and fails on the last two
bash refuses to run because ls output cannot be expanded
Only `notes.txt` is processed because the loop stops at the first space
blocks.explain: The command substitution `$(ls *.txt)` is unquoted, so its output is word-split on whitespace, and `q3 report.txt` becomes two words. The fix is to let the glob produce the list directly: `for f in *.txt; do wc -l "$f"; done`. Globbing results are not split again.

blocks.question: In bash, `echo {1,2}-$((3+4))` prints what?
blocks.explain: Brace expansion runs first and makes two words, `1-$((3+4))` and `2-$((3+4))`. Arithmetic expansion then evaluates each to 7.

lessons.title: Writing scripts: arguments, tests, if, loops and functions

blocks.md: Once a command works, you can save it in a file and it becomes a **script**: a text file of commands that bash runs top to bottom, as if you had typed them. The first line is usually `#!/usr/bin/env bash`, the **shebang** (the name joins hash and bang, nicknames for its first two characters). It tells the kernel which interpreter runs the file, and `env` finds bash by searching PATH. Run a script with `bash backup.sh`, or give it the execute bit with `chmod +x backup.sh` (lesson 1) and run `./backup.sh`.

Inside a script, the command-line arguments are **positional parameters**: `$1` is the first argument, `$#` is how many there are, and `$2`, `$3` and so on are the next ones. `$0` is the name the script was run as. `"$@"` is all of them, each kept as its own word, which lesson 3 showed is the right way to pass them on. `shift` drops the first argument and renumbers the rest.

`if` does not evaluate a boolean. It **runs a command** and takes the `then` branch if that command's exit status is 0, otherwise the `else` branch. So `if grep -q root /etc/passwd; then ...` is ordinary code. To compare values you run a command built for that: `test`, also spelled `[`. `[` is a builtin whose last argument must be `]`, which is why the spaces in `[ "$n" -gt 3 ]` are required: every piece is a separate argument.

The operators come from the POSIX `test` utility:

- strings: `=` and `!=`; `-z s` is true if s is empty, `-n s` if it is not
- integers: `-eq`, `-ne`, `-lt`, `-le`, `-gt`, `-ge` (equal, not equal, less than, and so on)
- files: `-e` exists, `-f` regular file, `-d` directory, `-x` executable

Mixing up the families is a quiet bug: `=` compares text, so `[ 01 = 1 ]` is false while `[ 01 -eq 1 ]` is true.

Bash adds its own `[[ ... ]]`, a keyword rather than a command. The words inside it are not word-split or globbed, so an empty or spaced variable cannot break it. It also adds `==` against a glob pattern (`[[ $f == *.log ]]`) and `=~` against a regular expression. Inside `[[ ]]`, `<` compares strings by sort order; inside `[ ]`, the same `<` is an input redirection.

blocks.code:
$ type [ [[ test
[ is a shell builtin
[[ is a shell keyword
test is a shell builtin
$ x=
$ [ $x = foo ]; echo "status $?"
bash: [: =: unary operator expected
status 2
$ [ "$x" = foo ]; echo "status $?"
status 1
$ [[ $x = foo ]]; echo "status $?"
status 1
$ [ 10 < 9 ]; echo "status $?"
bash: 9: No such file or directory
status 1
$ [[ 10 < 9 ]]; echo "status $?"
status 0
$ [ 10 -lt 9 ]; echo "status $?"
status 1
blocks.caption: Real bash session. With x empty, `[ $x = foo ]` becomes `[ = foo ]`, a syntax error (status 2). `[ 10 < 9 ]` tries to read a file named 9. `[[ 10 < 9 ]]` is true because the text 10 sorts before 9.

blocks.question: With `name="Ana Lee"`, a script runs `if [ $name = admin ]; then echo yes; else echo no; fi`. What is printed?
options: no, because the strings differ
yes, because `[` compares only the first word
an error from `[` (too many arguments), then no
nothing, because bash refuses to run the if
blocks.explain: Unquoted, `$name` splits into Ana and Lee, so `[` receives `Ana Lee = admin ]`, which is not a valid expression. It prints `[: too many arguments` and returns 2, and any non-zero status sends if to the else branch (real bash run). Quoting gives `[ "Ana Lee" = admin ]`, a clean false.

blocks.md: Loops repeat a body. `for x in a b c; do ...; done` runs once per word: use `for f in "$@"` for the arguments and `for f in *.log` for files (glob results are not split again). `while cmd; do ...; done` repeats as long as cmd succeeds. The safe way to process a file line by line is `while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file`. `read` reads one line into the variable and fails at end of file; `IFS=` (an empty separator, for this command only) stops it trimming leading and trailing spaces, and `-r` keeps backslashes as ordinary characters.

blocks.title: Reading a file line by line with while read
blocks.code:
n=0
while IFS= read -r line; do
  n=$((n+1))
  printf '%d: [%s]\n' "$n" "$line"
done < hosts.txt
echo "total $n"

scenes.caption: hosts.txt has three lines: `web1`, `  db1` (two leading spaces) and `C:\temp`. The redirection on line 5 feeds the file to the whole loop as its input (standard input, lesson 5). n starts at 0.
read takes the first line into `line` and succeeds, so the body runs: n becomes 1 and printf shows the line in brackets.
Second line. Because IFS is empty for this read, the two leading spaces are kept.
Third line. With -r the backslash is an ordinary character and stays in the value.
read reaches end of file and returns a non-zero status, so while stops and line 6 prints the count. Real output from bash.

blocks.code:
$ while read line; do printf '[%s]\n' "$line"; done < hosts.txt
[web1]
[db1]
[C:temp]
blocks.caption: The same file read without `IFS=` and `-r` (real output): the leading spaces are trimmed and the backslash is treated as an escape and disappears.

blocks.md: A **function** names a group of commands: `name() { commands; }`. Calling it looks like running a command, but it runs inside the current shell with no new process (lesson 2). Inside it, `$1`, `$#` and the rest refer to the function's own arguments. Variables are shared with the rest of the script unless declared with `local`. A function hands back two separate things: an **exit status**, set by `return N` (0 to 255) or else by its last command, and **output**, which the caller captures with `$(...)`.

blocks.caption: Real bash session. Output travels through `$(...)`; the status travels through `$?`, here the status of the command substitution.

blocks.md: Now a worked example. `backup.sh` should take directories as arguments, copy each one into a folder named after today's date, and warn about arguments that are not directories. `date +%F` prints the date as year-month-day. Here is a first attempt, run on a folder holding the directories `my docs` and `src`:

blocks.code:
$ cat naive.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
dest=backup-$(date +%F)
mkdir -p $dest
for d in $*; do
  cp -r $d $dest
done
echo "done"
$ ./naive.sh 'my docs' src missing; echo "status $?"
cp: my: No such file or directory
cp: docs: No such file or directory
cp: missing: No such file or directory
done
status 0
$ ls backup-*
src
blocks.caption: Real run on macOS (GNU cp on Linux words the errors as `cp: cannot stat 'my': No such file or directory`). Only src was copied, the errors scrolled past, and the script still said done with status 0.

blocks.md: Three bugs show in that run. The unquoted `$*` split `my docs` into `my` and `docs`. The failures were reported, yet the script printed done and exited 0, so anything that calls it would believe the backup worked. And with no arguments at all it would quietly create an empty backup folder. The fixed version checks `$#`, quotes every expansion, tests each argument with `-d`, sends warnings to standard error, skips to the next argument with `continue`, and remembers any failure in `status` to exit with it.

blocks.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
if [ "$#" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "usage: $0 DIR..." >&2
  exit 2
fi
dest="backup-$(date +%F)"
mkdir -p "$dest"
status=0
for d in "$@"; do
  if [ ! -d "$d" ]; then
    echo "warning: skipping $d (not a directory)" >&2
    status=1
    continue
  fi
  cp -r "$d" "$dest/"
  echo "copied $d"
done
exit "$status"
blocks.caption: backup.sh. Lesson 8 adds strict mode on top of this.

blocks.code:
$ ./backup.sh 'my docs' src missing; echo "status $?"
copied my docs
copied src
warning: skipping missing (not a directory)
status 1
$ ls backup-*
my docs
src
$ ./backup.sh; echo "status $?"
usage: ./backup.sh DIR...
status 2
blocks.caption: Real run in the same folder. The spaced name survives, the missing directory is reported on standard error, and the exit status tells a caller that something was skipped.

blocks.md: Inside `[ ]`, quote every variable: `[ "$x" = foo ]`. An empty or spaced value otherwise changes how many arguments `[` receives, and the test fails with an error instead of returning false. Inside `[[ ]]` a variable needs no quotes, except on the right of `==` or `=~`: there quotes make the pattern literal, so `[[ $f == "*.log" ]]` matches only a file named `*.log`.
`if`, `while`, `&&` and `||` all branch on an exit status. `[` and `test` are commands that turn a comparison into a status. Functions return a status with `return` and data on standard output.

blocks.question: After `f() { echo 5; return 3; }` and `y=$(f)`, what are y and `$?`?
options: y is 5 and `$?` is 3
y is 3 and `$?` is 0
y is 5 and `$?` is 0
y is 53 and `$?` is 0
blocks.explain: Command substitution captures what f prints, 5. The return value is not output; it becomes the exit status, and an assignment whose value came from `$(...)` takes that command's status, 3 (a real bash run printed `y=5 status=3`).

lessons.title: File descriptors: why the order of 2>&1 matters

blocks.md: Every process holds a table of **file descriptors** (fds): small integers that name open files, terminals or pipes. By convention fd 0 is **standard input**, fd 1 is **standard output** and fd 2 is **standard error** (stdin, stdout and stderr for short). A program like `ls` just writes results to fd 1 and complaints to fd 2; it neither knows nor cares where they lead.

Redirections are instructions the shell applies to the child's fd table after `fork` and before `exec`, and the table survives the exec. The core forms:

- `> file`, one greater-than sign: open file for writing on fd 1, truncating it (emptying it first)
- `>> file`, two greater-than signs: same, but append to the end
- `< file`, a less-than sign: open file for reading on fd 0
- `2> file`, the digit 2 then a greater-than sign: open file on fd 2
- `2>&1`: make fd 2 a **copy** of whatever fd 1 points to *right now*

The ampersand marks a file descriptor number: in `2>&1` the target after the greater-than sign is fd 1, while `2>1`, without the ampersand, would write to a file named 1. Redirections are processed left to right, and the word *copy* is the whole story of the next figure.

blocks.prompt: Which command sends both normal output and errors into the file `out`: `ls nosuch > out 2>&1` or `ls nosuch 2>&1 > out`?
blocks.reveal: Only the **first**. In the second, `2>&1` runs while fd 1 still points at the terminal, so fd 2 becomes a copy of the terminal. Then `> out` moves fd 1 alone. The error message `ls: nosuch: No such file or directory` appears on screen and `out` stays empty. The bash manual uses the same pair, written `ls > dirlist 2>&1` and `ls 2>&1 > dirlist`. (The error text shown is from macOS; GNU ls on Linux prints `ls: cannot access 'nosuch': No such file or directory`.)

blocks.title: The fd table of ls under two redirection orders

scenes.caption: After fork, the child inherits the shell's table: fds 0, 1 and 2 all point at the terminal. Indices are fd numbers.
First redirection. Top: `> out` opens the file on fd 1. Bottom: `2>&1` copies fd 1 into fd 2, but fd 1 is still the terminal, so nothing visible changes.
Second redirection. Top: `2>&1` copies fd 1, which now points at the file. Bottom: `> out` moves only fd 1. Errors on the bottom row still reach the screen.

blocks.md: Under the hood `2>&1` is the `dup2` system call: it makes fd 2 refer to the same open file as fd 1. The name is short for duplicate. They then share one file offset (the position where the next write lands), so output and errors interleave in the file in the order they were written instead of overwriting each other. Opening the same file twice (`> out 2> out`) gives two independent offsets that clobber each other.

blocks.code:
cmd > out.log 2>&1      # stdout and stderr to a file
cmd 2> /dev/null         # discard errors only
cmd < input.txt          # read stdin from a file
cmd >> out.log 2>&1     # append both
cmd 2>&1 | less          # page both through a pipe
cat <<'EOF' > config.ini
[server]
port = 8080
EOF
blocks.caption: Common redirection patterns. `/dev/null` is a special file that discards everything written to it, and `less` is a pager that shows text a screen at a time. In the last one, a *here-document* feeds the lines up to EOF as stdin; quoting 'EOF' disables expansion inside it.

blocks.md: The pipe line above works because of the same ordering rule. The shell connects the pipe to fd 1 before it processes the command's own redirections, so `2>&1` then copies the pipe into fd 2.

Three more tools build on redirection. `tee file` copies its standard input both to the file and to its standard output, so you can save a stream and keep piping it. It also fixes a classic surprise: in `sudo echo 3 > file` (sudo runs one command as another user, by default the administrator, root), your own unprivileged shell opens the file before sudo runs, and gets permission denied; in `echo 3 | sudo tee file`, the privileged tee opens it. Bash also has shorthands: `&> file` means `> file 2>&1`, `&>> file` appends both, and `cmd1 |& cmd2` means `cmd1 2>&1 | cmd2`. They are not POSIX sh (zsh has them too), and the old bash 3.2 that macOS ships rejects `&>>` and `|&`.

A **here-document** `<<WORD` feeds the lines that follow, up to a line containing only WORD, to the command's standard input. If WORD is unquoted, those lines are expanded like a double-quoted string: variables, `$(...)` and arithmetic are replaced. If any part of WORD is quoted, as in `<<'EOF'`, the lines pass through exactly as written.

blocks.code:
$ cat demo.sh
name=Ana
cat <<EOF
hi $name, 6 x 7 = $((6*7))
EOF
cat <<'EOF'
hi $name, 6 x 7 = $((6*7))
EOF
ls sub nosuch &> both.txt
cat both.txt
echo hello | tee copy.txt | tr a-z A-Z
cat copy.txt
$ bash demo.sh
hi Ana, 6 x 7 = 42
hi $name, 6 x 7 = $((6*7))
ls: nosuch: No such file or directory
sub:
a.txt
HELLO
hello
blocks.caption: Real run (macOS). `&>` put the error and the listing of the folder `sub` into one file. tee saved `hello` in copy.txt while passing it on to `tr`, which upper-cased it.

blocks.prompt: A script that generates a config file contains `cat <<EOF > run.sh` followed by the line `echo "user is $USER"`. When run.sh later runs on another account, whose name does it print?
blocks.reveal: **The name of whoever generated the file.** With an unquoted delimiter, `$USER` was expanded while the here-document was read, so run.sh contains the literal name. To keep `$USER` for run.sh to expand later, quote the delimiter: `cat <<'EOF' > run.sh`.

blocks.md: Misconception: `2>&1` *links* stderr to stdout permanently. It does not. It is a one-time copy of fd 1 as it is at that moment. Any later change to fd 1 leaves fd 2 where it was.

blocks.question: You want to keep only the errors of `make` in `errors.txt` and still see normal output on the terminal. Which works?
options: `make > errors.txt`
`make 2>&1 > errors.txt`
`make 2> errors.txt`
`make > errors.txt 2>&1`
blocks.explain: `2>` redirects fd 2 alone. The first option captures normal output instead, the last captures both, and `2>&1 > errors.txt` leaves errors on the terminal and puts normal output in the file, the opposite of what you want.

blocks.question: `grep -c error app.log > count.txt` prints `grep: app.log: No such file or directory` on the terminal. Why is that message not in count.txt?
options: count.txt is opened only after grep succeeds
grep prints errors through the shell, not through a file descriptor
Error messages go to fd 2, and only fd 1 was redirected
Redirection is ignored when the command fails
blocks.explain: The shell opens count.txt on fd 1 before exec, whether or not grep succeeds (so count.txt now exists, empty). grep writes its complaint to fd 2, which still points at the terminal.

lessons.title: Pipes: concurrent processes, sort | uniq -c, and SIGPIPE

blocks.md: A **pipe** is a one-way byte channel inside the kernel with a write end and a read end. In `a | b`, the shell creates a pipe, forks both commands, connects a's fd 1 to the write end and b's fd 0 to the read end, then waits for both. Each command is a separate process, and they all run **at the same time**: data streams through as it is produced, not after the first command finishes.

That composability is the Unix idea: small tools that read text on stdin and write text on stdout. Take this 9-line web server log, `access.log`, and ask which client IP addresses made the most requests. An IP (Internet Protocol) address names a machine on a network; in the common IPv4 form it is four numbers from 0 to 255 joined by dots, such as 10.0.0.1, and each number is one byte, called an octet.

blocks.caption: access.log: one request per line, client IP address first.

blocks.code:
cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 2
      4 10.0.0.1
      3 10.0.0.2
blocks.caption: Field 1 of each line, sorted, counted, sorted by count descending, top 2. Output from running it on the 9-line file.

blocks.title: What flows through each pipe (last octet of the address)

scenes.caption: `cut -d' ' -f1` keeps the first space-separated field of each line: 9 addresses in log order. Only the last octet is shown.
`sort` groups identical lines together. It must read all its input before writing anything, since the last line could sort first.
`uniq -c` collapses runs of **adjacent** equal lines and prefixes a count: 4 lines out. Shown as count x IP.
`sort -rn` orders by the leading number, largest first (-n numeric, -r reverse), and `head -n 2` keeps the top two.

blocks.md: Every flag in the pipeline above comes from the tool's manual page (lesson 1): `cut -d' ' -f1` sets the delimiter to a space and keeps field 1; `sort -n` compares numerically and `-r` reverses the order; `head -n 2` keeps the first two lines. `man sort` lists the rest. Lesson 7 does the same job with a single awk program.

blocks.prompt: What if you drop the first `sort` and run `cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | uniq -c` directly?
blocks.reveal: You get **9 lines, each with count 1**. uniq only merges *adjacent* duplicates (its man page: it does not detect repeated lines unless they are adjacent), and in this log no address appears twice in a row. That is why `sort | uniq -c` is a fixed idiom.

blocks.title: Request counts per IP address: with and without sort

scenes.caption: Correct pipeline: `sort | uniq -c` gives each address's total.
Without sort, the largest count uniq ever reports for any address is 1, because no two equal lines are adjacent. The result looks plausible and is wrong.

blocks.md: Pipes have finite capacity. If the writer is faster than the reader, the pipe fills and the writer's `write` call blocks until the reader catches up. Linux has used a default capacity of 16 pages since kernel version 2.6.11. A page is the fixed-size block in which the kernel manages memory, usually 4,096 bytes: 4 x 1,024, written 4 KiB because a kibibyte is 1,024 bytes. So the pipe holds 16 x 4,096 = 65,536 bytes, though the man page says programs should not rely on a particular size. When the writer closes its end, the reader sees end of file.

The opposite case: the reader exits early. A **signal** is a numbered notification the kernel delivers to a process, and each signal has a default action. When the reader is gone, the writer's next write to the pipe makes the kernel send it **SIGPIPE**, the broken-pipe signal, whose default action kills it. `yes` prints `y` forever, yet `yes | head -n 1` ends at once. When a process dies from signal number N, bash reports status 128 + N; SIGPIPE is signal 13, so `yes` ends with 141. Bash saves every stage's status in the array variable `PIPESTATUS`, first stage first, so after `yes | head -n 1` it holds 141 and 0.

blocks.title: yes | head -n 1 (simplified ordering, not to scale)

scenes.caption: Both processes start together. yes writes lines of `y` into the pipe; head blocks in read until data arrives.
head reads a chunk, prints the first line, closes the read end and exits with status 0.
yes's next write finds no reader. The kernel sends SIGPIPE and yes dies. bash records `PIPESTATUS` as `141 0`.

blocks.md: A pipeline is several processes running concurrently and connected by bounded kernel buffers. Fast writers block on a full pipe; writers to a closed pipe get SIGPIPE. Tools like `sort` that need all their input are where a pipeline stops streaming.

blocks.question: `grep ERROR huge.log | head -n 5` returns almost instantly even though huge.log is 50 GB. Why?
options: grep detects the head command and reads only 5 lines
head reads the file directly and grep is skipped
The kernel caches the whole file before grep starts
Once head exits after 5 lines, grep's next write raises SIGPIPE and grep dies
blocks.explain: Both run concurrently. After head has its five lines it exits, closing the read end. grep's next write to the pipe triggers SIGPIPE, ending it long before it reaches the end of the file.

blocks.question: Which pipeline lists the 3 most common words in words.txt (one word per line)?
options: `uniq -c words.txt | sort -rn | head -n 3`
`sort words.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3`
`sort -rn words.txt | uniq -c | head -n 3`
`sort words.txt | head -n 3 | uniq -c`
blocks.explain: Sort first so equal words are adjacent, count with uniq -c, then sort the counts numerically in reverse and take 3. The third option sorts the words themselves, not counts, and the last one cuts the data before counting.

lessons.title: Searching and transforming text: grep, regex, find, sed and awk

blocks.md: Lesson 6 built a pipeline from `cut`, `sort`, `uniq` and `head`. Four more tools cover most of the rest of everyday text work. `grep` prints the lines that match a pattern, `find` lists files by name, type or age, `sed` (stream editor) rewrites each line as it streams past, and `awk` is a small language for fields and totals. The patterns that grep, sed and awk take are **regular expressions** (regex for short): a compact language that describes a set of strings.

A regular expression is built from a few pieces (the POSIX rules in regex(7)):

- an ordinary character matches itself: `GET`
- `.` matches any single character
- `[abc]` matches one character from the set, `[a-c]` one from a range, `[^abc]` any character not listed
- after an item, `*` means zero or more of it, `+` one or more, `?` zero or one
- `^` matches at the start of the line and `$` at the end
- `( )` groups items and `|` separates alternatives: `(GET|POST)`
- a backslash makes a special character ordinary: `\.` is a literal dot

There are two dialects. **Basic** regular expressions (BRE), the default for grep and sed, treat `+`, `?`, `|`, `(` and `)` as ordinary characters. **Extended** regular expressions (ERE), selected with `grep -E` or `sed -E`, give them the meanings above. When a pattern containing `+` or `|` matches nothing, a missing `-E` is the usual cause. Always put the pattern in single quotes, so the shell passes `*`, `$` and spaces to the tool untouched (lesson 3).

blocks.title: Which lines of access.log each pattern matches

scenes.caption: The 9-line access.log from lesson 6, one column per line: last octet of the client address, method and path. Indices are line numbers.
`grep -n POST`: a literal pattern. Only line 5 contains the characters POST; -n prefixes each printed line with its number.
`grep ' /$'`: a space, a slash, then the end of the line. Lines 1, 4 and 6 request exactly /. Line 2 fails because a character follows the slash.
`grep -E '/[a-c]$'`: a slash, then one character from a to c, then the end of the line. Lines 2, 3 and 5 match.
`grep -c '^10\.0\.0\.1 '`: the address 10.0.0.1 at the start of the line, then a space. The escaped dots are literal dots. Count: 4 (lines 1, 3, 5 and 9).
`grep -oE '/[a-z]+$'`: -o prints only the matched part. Lines whose path is a bare / have no letter after the slash and print nothing; the other six print /a to /f.

blocks.code:
$ grep -n POST access.log
5:10.0.0.1 POST /c
$ grep -n ' /$' access.log
1:10.0.0.1 GET /
4:10.0.0.3 GET /
6:10.0.0.2 GET /
$ grep -nE '/[a-c]$' access.log
2:10.0.0.2 GET /a
3:10.0.0.1 GET /b
5:10.0.0.1 POST /c
$ grep -c '^10\.0\.0\.1 ' access.log
4
$ grep -oE '/[a-z]+$' access.log | tr '\n' ' '; echo
/a /b /c /d /e /f
$ grep -q DELETE access.log; echo "status $?"
status 1
$ grep DELETE nosuch.log; echo "status $?"
grep: nosuch.log: No such file or directory
status 2
blocks.caption: Real output on the 9-line access.log (BSD grep on macOS). `tr` replaces each newline with a space to keep the -o output on one line.

blocks.md: The options you will use most: `-n` line numbers, `-i` ignore case, `-v` invert (print the lines that do **not** match), `-c` count matching lines, `-o` print only the matched part, `-r` search a whole directory, `-q` print nothing. In scripts the exit status matters most: grep returns 0 if a line matched, 1 if none did, and 2 if an error occurred, such as a missing file. That is why `if grep -q TODO notes.txt` works, and where the status 2 in lesson 8's pipeline comes from.

blocks.prompt: `grep -c '^10.0.0.1' access.log`, with the dots not escaped, also prints 4. Is the pattern correct?
blocks.reveal: **No, it only happens to work.** An unescaped `.` matches any character, and nothing marks where the address ends. On three lines starting `10.0.0.15`, `10a0b0c1` and `10.0.0.1`, it counts all three; `'^10\.0\.0\.1 '`, with escaped dots and a trailing space, counts only the last one (both checked with a real run). Patterns that look right on your sample can be wrong on the next file.

blocks.md: `find` walks a directory tree and tests every entry it meets. `find logs -name '*.log' -type f` lists the regular files under logs whose name matches the glob; quote the glob so that find, not the shell, does the matching. `-type d` selects directories and `-mtime -7` files modified less than 7 days (7 x 24 hours) ago. By default find prints each path. `-exec cmd {} +` runs cmd with the found paths in place of `{}`, many per run, while `-exec cmd {} \;` runs it once per file. For names with spaces, `-print0 | xargs -0` from lesson 3 is the other safe route.

blocks.code:
$ find . -name '*.log' | sort
./access.log
./logs/app.log
./logs/err.log
./logs/old/jan 1.log
$ find logs -name '*.log' -exec wc -l {} + | sort
       1 logs/old/jan 1.log
       2 logs/err.log
       3 logs/app.log
       6 total
$ find . -name *.log
./access.log
$ touch debug.log
$ find . -name *.log
find: debug.log: unknown primary or operator
blocks.caption: Real run with BSD find on macOS. Unquoted, `*.log` is expanded by the shell before find starts: with one match in the current folder find silently searches only for `access.log`; with two it fails. GNU find on Linux says `paths must precede expression` instead.

blocks.md: `sed` reads lines, applies editing commands to each, and prints the result; the input file is not changed. Its workhorse is substitution: `s/old/new/` replaces the first match on each line and `s/old/new/g` every match. With `-E`, parentheses in the pattern **capture** the text they match, and `\1`, `\2` in the replacement insert those captures, so you can reorder parts of a line.

blocks.code:
$ sed 's/GET/get/' access.log | head -n 2
10.0.0.1 get /
10.0.0.2 get /a
$ sed -E 's/^([0-9.]+) (GET|POST) (.*)/\2 \3 from \1/' access.log | head -n 3
GET / from 10.0.0.1
GET /a from 10.0.0.2
GET /b from 10.0.0.1
blocks.caption: Real output. The second command captures the address, the method and the rest of the line, then writes them back in a different order.

blocks.md: `sed -i` edits a file in place, and it differs between systems. GNU sed (Linux) takes an optional backup suffix glued to the flag, so `sed -i 's/a/b/' f` works. BSD sed (macOS) requires the suffix argument, so the same command takes the script as the suffix and fails. `sed -i.bak 's/a/b/' f` works on both and keeps the original as `f.bak`.

`awk` runs a small program on every line. A program is a list of `pattern { action }` pairs, and for each line (awk calls it a **record**) every pattern that is true runs its action; a missing pattern matches every line. awk splits the line on whitespace into **fields** `$1`, `$2` and so on up to `$NF`, where NF is the number of fields, while `$0` is the whole line and NR the record number. `BEGIN { }` runs before the first line and `END { }` after the last. Variables need no declaration and start empty, and arrays are **associative**: indexed by strings, so `c["10.0.0.1"]` is a valid slot.

blocks.code:
$ awk '{ print $3 }' access.log | head -n 3
/
/a
/b
$ awk '$2 == "POST" { print NR ": " $0 }' access.log
5: 10.0.0.1 POST /c
$ awk 'END { print NR " lines" }' access.log
9 lines
$ awk '{ c[$1]++ } END { for (ip in c) print c[ip], ip }' access.log | sort -rn
4 10.0.0.1
3 10.0.0.2
1 10.0.0.4
1 10.0.0.3
blocks.caption: Real output (macOS awk). The last command answers lesson 6's question, which addresses made the most requests, with one awk program instead of `cut | sort | uniq -c`: the same counts.

blocks.title: awk counting requests per address in one pass

scenes.caption: Record 1: `$1` is 10.0.0.1. `c[$1]++` adds 1 to that array slot, which starts empty and counts as 0.
After record 3, address 10.0.0.1 has been seen twice and 10.0.0.2 once.
After record 6, every address seen so far has its own slot, created on first use.
After record 9, the last line: the same totals that `sort | uniq -c` produced, built in one pass with no sorting.
END runs once, after the input. `for (ip in c)` visits keys in an unspecified order, so the pipeline sorts the result with `sort -rn`; the output shown is after that sort.

blocks.md: grep selects lines, sed rewrites them, awk computes over fields, and find selects files. Single-quote every pattern so the shell leaves it alone, and add `-E` when you want `+`, `?`, `|` or groups.

blocks.question: Why does `grep -c '.' notes.txt` count every line except the empty ones?
options: `.` matches a literal dot, and most lines end with one
grep skips empty lines in every search
`-c` counts characters, not lines
`.` matches any single character, so any line with at least one character matches
blocks.explain: In a regex, `.` is any one character, and a line matches if the pattern matches anywhere in it. Every non-empty line qualifies and only empty lines fail: a real run on the lines `ab`, an empty line and `c` prints 2. To match a literal dot, escape it: `'\.'`.

blocks.question: In a folder containing `a.txt` and `b.txt`, `find . -name *.txt` fails with an error. Why?
options: find does not accept globs after -name
-name needs the full path rather than a pattern
The shell expands `*.txt` to `a.txt b.txt` before find runs, so find gets an extra argument it cannot parse
find refuses to search the current directory
blocks.explain: Expansion happens before the command runs (lesson 3). find receives `-name a.txt b.txt`; -name takes exactly one pattern, so `b.txt` is a stray argument. `find . -name '*.txt'` passes the pattern through for find to match against every file name in the tree.

lessons.title: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly

blocks.md: Every command returns an **exit status** from 0 to 255. Zero means success and anything else is failure; the bash manual explains this is so there is one well-defined way to succeed and many ways to fail. `$?` holds the last status. The operators `&&` and `||` branch on it: `make && ./app` runs the app only if make succeeded, and `cd dir || exit 1` stops if cd failed.

blocks.title: Exit statuses you will meet, and what they mean

scenes.caption: 0 is success. Programs choose their own failure codes, commonly 1; bash builtins use 2 for incorrect usage such as an invalid option.
126 and 127 come from the shell itself: the file was found but could not be executed, or nothing by that name was found at all.

Above 128 means death by a signal: subtract 128 to get the signal number. SIGINT (interrupt, sent by Ctrl-C) is 2, SIGPIPE 13, SIGTERM (terminate, the default of kill) 15, in Linux numbering. All values were reproduced in bash.

blocks.md:
By default a bash script ignores failures and keeps going: if `cd build` fails, the following `rm -rf *` runs in the wrong directory. Three options make scripts stop instead. They are usually written together as `set -euo pipefail` right after the shebang line (`#!/usr/bin/env bash`, from lesson 4):

- `-e`: exit as soon as a command fails
- `-u`: treat expanding an unset variable as an error
- `-o pipefail`: a pipeline fails if **any** stage fails, not just the last

blocks.prompt: Without pipefail, what is the status of `false | true`? And of `grep foo missing.txt | wc -l`?
blocks.reveal: Both are **0**. By default a pipeline's status is the status of its **last** command, and `true` and `wc` both succeed. The grep error message prints, wc prints 0, and a script happily continues. With `set -o pipefail` the statuses become 1 and 2: the rightmost non-zero status.

blocks.md: `-e` has exceptions that surprise everyone, and they are deliberate. The shell does not exit when the failing command is the condition of an `if`, `while` or `until`, part of an `&&` or `||` list except the last command, any pipeline stage but the last (unless pipefail), or negated with `!`. Worse, a function called in such a context runs its *whole body* with `-e` ignored.

blocks.title: Which lines run under set -euo pipefail?
blocks.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
f() { false; echo "still in f"; }
f || echo "f failed"
false && echo "never printed"
echo "after the && list"
grep foo missing.txt | wc -l
echo "never reached"

scenes.caption: Line 2 turns the options on. Line 3 only defines a function; nothing in it runs yet.
`f` is called on the left of `||`, so -e is ignored inside its whole body. The `false` in f does not stop it, and `still in f` prints. f returns 0, so `f failed` never prints.

blocks.md: `set -e` is a safety net, not error handling. It misses failures inside functions called from conditions and in `&&` chains. For steps that matter, check explicitly: `if ! cp src dst; then echo 'copy failed' >&2; exit 1; fi`.

blocks.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

if [ "$#" -ne 1 ]; then
  echo "usage: $0 LOGFILE" >&2
  exit 2
fi
log="$1"

# top 3 client IPs
cut -d' ' -f1 "$log" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3
blocks.caption: top-ips.sh: strict mode, quoted expansions, usage errors on fd 2 with a non-zero status, and a pipeline. Give it the execute bit with `chmod +x top-ips.sh` (lesson 1), then run `./top-ips.sh access.log`.

blocks.md: pipefail meets SIGPIPE: with pipefail on, `yes | head -n 1` has status 141, because yes was killed when head exited. `seq 1 3 | head -n 1` (seq prints the numbers 1 to 3) returns 0 only because all its output fit in the pipe before head quit. Under `set -e`, a producer piped into `head` can end the script on large inputs; test such pipelines at realistic sizes.

Two tools catch the mistakes this course has warned about before they bite. [ShellCheck](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck) is a static analysis tool for shell scripts: it reads the script without running it and flags unquoted expansions, broken tests and subtler traps. One of them defeats `set -e` silently. In `local cfg=$(cat "$1")`, the status of the line is the status of `local`, which succeeds, so a failing cat is ignored ([SC2155](https://www.shellcheck.net/wiki/SC2155)). Declaring and assigning on separate lines keeps the real status.

blocks.code:
$ cat deploy.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
load() {
  local cfg=$(cat "$1")
  echo "loaded ${#cfg} bytes"
}
dir=$1
load $dir/app.conf
$ bash deploy.sh nowhere; echo "status $?"
cat: nowhere/app.conf: No such file or directory
loaded 0 bytes
status 0
$ shellcheck deploy.sh

In deploy.sh line 4:
  local cfg=$(cat "$1")
        ^-^ SC2155 (warning): Declare and assign separately to avoid masking return values.


In deploy.sh line 8:
load $dir/app.conf
     ^--^ SC2086 (info): Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting.

Did you mean:
load "$dir"/app.conf
blocks.caption: Real run (ShellCheck 0.11.0; its trailing links to the wiki pages are cut). Even under strict mode the missing file goes unnoticed and the script exits 0. Writing `local cfg` and then `cfg=$(cat "$1")` makes the same call exit with status 1.

blocks.md: When a script misbehaves at run time, `bash -x script.sh` (or `set -x` inside it) prints every command **after expansion** on standard error, prefixed with `+`, before running it. Arguments containing spaces are shown in quotes, so you can count exactly what each command received. Command substitutions show up one level deeper, as `++`.

blocks.code:
$ cat trace.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
f="my app"
n=$((2 + 3))
ls "$f"
ls $f
$ bash -x trace.sh
+ f='my app'
+ n=5
+ ls 'my app'
app.conf
+ ls my app
ls: app: No such file or directory
ls: my: No such file or directory
blocks.caption: Real trace on macOS (GNU ls on Linux words the errors as `ls: cannot access 'my': No such file or directory`). `+ ls 'my app'` is one argument; `+ ls my app` is two, which is the unquoted `$f` being word-split.

blocks.md: Status 0 means success; 128 + N means killed by signal N. Start scripts with `set -euo pipefail`, quote every expansion, send errors to fd 2, and exit non-zero on failure so the next tool in the chain can tell.

blocks.question: A script has `set -e`. Its line `grep -q TODO notes.txt && echo found` runs when notes.txt has no TODO. What happens?
options: The script exits with status 1 because grep failed
Nothing prints and the script continues with the next line
The script exits with status 127
The echo runs because && ignores failures under -e
blocks.explain: grep is not the final command of the `&&` list, so its failure is exempt from -e. The echo is skipped and execution continues. (If this were the last line, the script's own exit status would still be 1.)

blocks.question: A CI step runs `pytest | tee test.log` (tee copies its input to the screen and to a file) and always shows green even when tests fail. What is the minimal fix?
options: Replace `|` with `&&`
Add `set -u`
Add `set -o pipefail` before the command
Redirect with `2>&1` instead of piping
blocks.explain: The pipeline's status is tee's, which succeeds. pipefail makes the pipeline report the rightmost non-zero status, so pytest's failure surfaces. `&&` would stop tee from seeing the output stream at all.

blocks.question: Under `bash -x`, a script prints `+ cp my report.txt /backup`. How many arguments did cp receive, and what does that suggest?
options: Three: `my`, `report.txt` and `/backup`, so a variable holding `my report.txt` was not quoted
Two, because the trace shows the line as written in the script
One, the whole text after cp
It cannot be known from a trace
blocks.explain: The trace prints each command after expansion and quotes any argument that contains a space, as in `+ ls 'my app'`. No quotes around `my report.txt` means word splitting produced two words. Quote the expansion: `cp "$f" /backup`.

lessons.title: Job control and signals: Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z, background jobs and trap

blocks.md:
Every running program is a process with a number, its **process ID** (PID); `ps` lists processes. Lesson 6 introduced **signals**, numbered notifications the kernel delivers to a process, through SIGPIPE, and lesson 8 decoded status 128 + N as death by signal N. Signals are also how you control programs from the terminal:

- **SIGINT** (2), sent by Ctrl-C: interrupt
- **SIGTSTP**, sent by Ctrl-Z: stop typed at the terminal, a pause
- **SIGCONT**: continue a stopped process
- **SIGTERM** (15): a request to terminate, the default signal of `kill`
- **SIGKILL** (9): terminate, and it cannot be caught or ignored
- **SIGHUP** (1): hangup, the terminal went away

Bash runs one **foreground** job at a time: the job that owns the terminal and receives what you type. Ending a command with `&` starts it in the **background**: bash prints a job number and a PID and gives the prompt back at once. `jobs` lists your jobs, `fg %1` brings job 1 to the foreground, and `bg %1` lets a stopped job continue in the background. Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Z reach only the foreground **process group** (the processes of the foreground job), so background jobs never see them.

blocks.title: One job: foreground, stopped, background, killed (not to scale)

scenes.caption: `sleep 100` starts in the foreground. It owns the terminal, and bash waits for it, so there is no prompt.
Ctrl-Z sends SIGTSTP. The job stops: still in memory, using no CPU. Bash prints Stopped and gives the prompt back.
`bg %1` sends SIGCONT and the job continues in the background, while the prompt stays free for other commands such as `ls`.
`kill %1` sends SIGTERM. sleep has no handler for it, so it ends; bash reports it Terminated, and its status is 143 (128 + 15).

blocks.code:
$ sleep 100
^Z
[1]+  Stopped                 sleep 100
$ jobs
[1]+  Stopped                 sleep 100
$ bg %1
[1]+ sleep 100 &
$ jobs
[1]+  Running                 sleep 100 &
$ sleep 200 &
[2] 78545
$ jobs -l
[1]- 78313 Running                 sleep 100 &
[2]+ 78545 Running                 sleep 200 &
$ kill %1
$ jobs
[1]-  Terminated: 15          sleep 100
[2]+  Running                 sleep 200 &
$ kill -9 %2
$ jobs
[2]+  Killed: 9               sleep 200
blocks.caption: A real interactive bash session (bash 3.2 on macOS; the wording of the status lines varies between systems). `^Z` is the terminal's echo of Ctrl-Z. `jobs -l` adds PIDs, and `+` marks the current job, the default for fg and bg.

blocks.md: `kill PID`, or `kill %1` for a job, sends SIGTERM unless you name another signal. A program may catch SIGTERM to finish writing, delete its temporary files and exit cleanly. `kill -9` sends SIGKILL, which cannot be caught, blocked or ignored: the kernel ends the process at once, so none of that cleanup runs. To turn a status back into a signal name, `kill -l 143` prints TERM.

blocks.prompt: A script runs `sleep 30 & pid=$!`, then `kill "$pid"`, `wait "$pid"` and `echo $?`. What does it print, and what changes with `kill -9`?
blocks.reveal: **143**, which is 128 + 15 for SIGTERM. With `kill -9` it prints **137**, 128 + 9. `$!` holds the PID of the most recent background job, and `wait PID` waits for that process and returns its exit status. Both values come from a real bash run, which also printed `Terminated: 15` and `Killed: 9` notices (macOS wording; with glibc on Linux they read `Terminated` and `Killed`).

blocks.md: Closing the terminal window, or losing an ssh connection, sends **SIGHUP** to the shell. Bash then resends SIGHUP to all its jobs, running or stopped, and the default action of SIGHUP is to terminate. Two ways out: start the command as `nohup cmd &`, which makes it ignore SIGHUP and, if its output was the terminal, appends it to `nohup.out`; or, for a job that is already running, `disown %1`, which removes it from bash's job table so bash does not pass the signal on. Lesson 10 shows the more convenient tool, tmux.

In scripts, `&` is a simple way to run things in parallel. Start several commands in the background, save each `$!`, then `wait` for each PID to collect its exit status. The total time is that of the slowest job, not the sum.

blocks.code:
$ cat par.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
sleep 3 & a=$!
sleep 2 & b=$!
( sleep 1; exit 3 ) & c=$!
wait "$a"; echo "a finished: status $?"
wait "$b"; echo "b finished: status $?"
wait "$c"; echo "c finished: status $?"
echo "total: ${SECONDS}s"
$ bash par.sh
a finished: status 0
b finished: status 0
c finished: status 3
total: 3s
blocks.caption: Real run. Jobs of 3, 2 and 1 seconds finish in 3 seconds in total (`SECONDS` counts seconds since the script started), and job c's own status, 3, comes back through wait.

blocks.md: A script that creates a temporary file should delete it on every exit path, Ctrl-C included. `mktemp` creates a file with a unique random name and prints that name. `trap 'commands' SIGNALS` registers commands for bash to run when one of the signals arrives, and the special name `EXIT` means whenever the shell exits. The usual pattern: put the cleanup in a function, trap it on EXIT, and turn INT and TERM into an ordinary `exit` with the matching 128 + N status, which in turn runs the EXIT trap.

blocks.code:
$ cat work.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
tmp=$(mktemp ./tmp.XXXXXX)
echo "working in $tmp"
sleep 100
rm -f "$tmp"
$ cat safe.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
tmp=$(mktemp ./tmp.XXXXXX)
cleanup() { rm -f "$tmp"; echo "removed $tmp"; }
trap cleanup EXIT
trap 'exit 130' INT
trap 'exit 143' TERM
echo "working in $tmp"
sleep 100
$ ./work.sh
working in ./tmp.rpCW58
^C
$ echo "status $?"; ls tmp.*
status 130
tmp.rpCW58
$ ./safe.sh
working in ./tmp.9YGvry
^Cremoved ./tmp.9YGvry
$ echo "status $?"; ls tmp.*
status 130
tmp.rpCW58
blocks.caption: Real session. After Ctrl-C (status 130 = 128 + 2), the script without a trap leaves its temporary file behind; safe.sh removes its own. `^C` is the echo of Ctrl-C.

blocks.md: Bash runs a trap only after the current foreground command finishes. If a script is inside `sleep 600` when SIGTERM arrives, its cleanup waits up to ten minutes. Run long commands as `cmd & wait $!` instead: `wait` returns as soon as a trapped signal arrives, and the trap runs right away. Have the cleanup also `kill` that background PID, or the command keeps running after the script exits.

Reaching for `kill -9` first is a habit worth breaking. SIGKILL gives the program no chance to flush buffered output, remove lock or temporary files, or stop its own child processes, which can be left running as orphans. Send SIGTERM, give it a few seconds, then escalate.
Ctrl-C is SIGINT, Ctrl-Z is SIGTSTP, `kill` is SIGTERM, `kill -9` is SIGKILL, and a closed terminal is SIGHUP. In a script, route every way out, signals included, through one `trap ... EXIT` cleanup.

blocks.question: You press Ctrl-Z while a long `make` runs, then type `ls`. What state is make in, and how do you let it continue while keeping your prompt?
options: It was killed; rerun it as `make &`
It keeps running in the background already, so nothing is needed
It is stopped; `bg` resumes it in the background
It is stopped; `fg` resumes it and keeps the prompt free
blocks.explain: Ctrl-Z sends SIGTSTP, which stops the process without ending it. `bg` sends SIGCONT and lets it run in the background while you keep the prompt. `fg` would also resume it, but in the foreground, taking the terminal back.

blocks.question: A script creates a file with mktemp and deletes it on its last line, with no trap. You press Ctrl-C halfway through. Why does the file survive?
options: mktemp files are protected from deletion until reboot
SIGINT ends the script before its last line runs, and no cleanup was registered
Ctrl-C stops only the current command, and the script then skips rm
rm cannot run while a signal is pending
blocks.explain: The default action of SIGINT is to terminate, so the script dies where it was and never reaches its `rm`. The real run above left `tmp.rpCW58` behind. With `trap cleanup EXIT` and `trap 'exit 130' INT`, bash runs the cleanup on the way out.

lessons.title: Your environment and remote machines: dotfiles, ssh and tmux

blocks.md: Settings you want in every shell, such as a longer PATH or your aliases, live in **startup files** that bash reads as it starts. They are **dotfiles**: plain text files whose names begin with a dot, so `ls` hides them (lesson 1). Which ones bash reads depends on two properties. A **login shell** is the first shell of a session, such as the one ssh starts when you log in. An **interactive** shell reads commands you type at a terminal, unlike a shell running a script.

The bash manual gives the rules:

- interactive **login** shell: read `/etc/profile`, then the **first** of `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login` and `~/.profile` that exists
- interactive **non-login** shell, for example after typing `bash`: read `~/.bashrc`
- non-interactive shell running a script: read neither (only a file named in the `BASH_ENV` variable)

So a line in `~/.bashrc` is invisible to a login shell unless `~/.bash_profile` reads it. A common fix is one line in `~/.bash_profile`: `if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then . ~/.bashrc; fi`, using `.` (source) from lesson 2 to run the file inside the current shell.

scenes.caption: You log in with ssh, and sshd starts a login shell. Bash reads /etc/profile, then only the first of the three files in your home directory that exists.
You type `bash` at a prompt: an interactive shell that is not a login shell. It reads ~/.bashrc and nothing else.
`./backup.sh` runs in a non-interactive shell: no startup file at all, so aliases from ~/.bashrc are absent. Only exported variables arrive, through the environment (lesson 2).
The usual setup: keep settings in ~/.bashrc and have ~/.bash_profile source it, so login and non-login interactive shells end up the same.

blocks.md: PATH (lesson 2) is the setting you will edit most. Add a directory in front and keep the old list: `export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"`. Writing `PATH=~/bin` would replace the whole list, and every ordinary command would become command not found. Check the result with `type -a name`, which lists every match in PATH order. An **alias** is a text shortcut for interactive typing, such as `alias ll='ls -l'`. Bash does not expand aliases in non-interactive shells, so scripts cannot rely on them; a function does everything an alias does and also takes arguments.

blocks.code:
$ hello
bash: hello: command not found
$ echo "status $?"
status 127
$ export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"
$ type -a hello
hello is /home/ana/bin/hello
$ hello
hello from ~/bin
$ cat usealias.sh
alias ll="ls -l"
ll
$ bash usealias.sh
usealias.sh: line 2: ll: command not found
blocks.caption: Real bash session with HOME pointing at a demo folder (its long path is shown here as /home/ana). The second half runs a two-line script that defines an alias and uses it; in a non-interactive shell the alias is never expanded.

blocks.prompt: On a server, you add `export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"` to `~/.bashrc`. Your `~/.bash_profile` exists but never mentions `.bashrc`. You log in with ssh and run a tool from `~/bin`. What happens?
blocks.reveal: **command not found.** ssh started a login shell, which read `~/.bash_profile` and stopped: a login shell reads only the first of the three login files, and never `~/.bashrc` on its own. Typing `bash` would start a non-login shell that does read it, which makes the bug confusing. The fix is to source `~/.bashrc` from `~/.bash_profile`.

blocks.md: **ssh** (secure shell) gives you a shell on another machine over an encrypted connection: `ssh ana@web1.example.com` logs in as the user ana. On the first connection ssh shows the fingerprint (a short hash) of the server's **host key**, the key that identifies that machine, and, once you accept it, records the key in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. If that key ever changes, ssh warns loudly, because it may mean another machine is pretending to be the server. Given a command, ssh runs it on the remote machine instead of a login shell and exits with its status, so remote and local tools combine with pipes. One startup-file exception: bash started by sshd to run such a command is not interactive, yet the bash manual says it still reads `~/.bashrc`.

Typing a password for every login is slow and can be guessed. A **key pair** replaces it. `ssh-keygen -t ed25519` creates two files: a **private key**, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, that never leaves your machine, and a **public key**, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`, that you add to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on the server, one key per line. To log in, the client proves it holds the private key by signing data with it, and the server checks the signature against a public key listed for that account (the publickey method of [RFC 4252](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4252)).

blocks.title: ssh login with a key pair (simplified from RFC 4252)

scenes.caption: The connection begins with a key exchange that sets up encryption and a session identifier unique to this connection. The server presents its host key, which ssh compares with ~/.ssh/known_hosts.
The client may first ask whether a public key would be accepted. sshd looks it up in the user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and answers PK_OK if it is listed.

add.label: may I use this public key?

scenes.caption: The client signs data that includes the session identifier, using the private key. The server checks the signature with the public key. Only the signature crosses the network, never the private key.
Authenticated, the session runs a login shell, or the single command you gave, and ssh exits with that command's status.

blocks.code:
$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ./demo_key -N '' -C ana@laptop
Generating public/private ed25519 key pair.
Your identification has been saved in ./demo_key
Your public key has been saved in ./demo_key.pub
The key fingerprint is:
SHA256:AJovCFzqZnWbWHEmyFBmHoOFU+LgmZbwZkxfdLctQ/M ana@laptop
...
$ ls -l demo_key demo_key.pub | cut -c1-10
-rw-------
-rw-r--r--
blocks.caption: Real run (OpenSSH on macOS). `-N ''` sets an empty passphrase for this demo only, and the `...` hides the randomart picture. The private key is created readable by its owner alone, mode 600.

blocks.md: Lesson 1's permissions matter here. ssh ignores a private key file that other users can access, and sshd refuses `authorized_keys` if the file, `~/.ssh` or your home directory is writable by other users (see [sshd(8)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/sshd.8.html)). Keep `~/.ssh` at 700 and the files in it at 600. For servers you use often, `~/.ssh/config` stores the details under a short name, and scp and rsync read it too. `scp` copies files over ssh; `rsync -a` does the same while preserving permissions and times, and sends only the differences from what is already on the other side, so repeating it is cheap.

blocks.code:
# ~/.ssh/config
Host web1
    HostName web1.example.com
    User ana
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

# then, from your laptop:
ssh web1                              # log in
ssh web1 'grep -c ERROR /var/log/app.log'   # count on the server
ssh web1 cat /var/log/app.log | sort  # sort on your laptop
scp report.txt web1:reports/          # copy a file over ssh
rsync -a site/ web1:/srv/site/        # copy only what changed
blocks.caption: A config entry and what it enables (the host name is an example). The quotes make the whole grep command run on the server; in the next line only cat runs there and sort runs on your laptop. A trailing slash on an rsync source means the contents of the directory.

blocks.md: A long job started over ssh dies with the connection: the remote shell receives SIGHUP and passes it to its jobs (lesson 9). A **terminal multiplexer** avoids this. **tmux** runs a server process on the remote machine that owns your shells; your terminal is only a client attached to it. Start a named session with `tmux new -s build`, run the job, press Ctrl-b and then d to **detach**, and log out. Later, ssh back in and run `tmux attach -t build`: the session and the job are still there. tmux also splits one terminal into windows and panes.

blocks.code:
$ tmux new -d -s build 'sleep 300'
$ tmux ls
build: 1 windows (created Sat Nov 14 00:59:35 2026)
blocks.caption: Real run. `-d` creates the session already detached; `tmux ls` lists sessions that are alive whether or not any terminal shows them.

blocks.md: The private key works like your password on every server that lists its public key. Never copy it to a server or commit it to a repository, and protect it with a passphrase; `ssh-agent` can hold the unlocked key so you type the passphrase once per session.

Login shells read ~/.bash_profile, other interactive shells ~/.bashrc, scripts neither. ssh logs you in with a key pair whose private half never leaves your machine, and tmux keeps remote work alive when the connection drops.

blocks.question: Which approach keeps a 3-hour job running if your ssh connection to the server drops?
options: Starting it as `./job.sh &` in the ssh session
Starting it inside tmux on your laptop, then running ssh in that tmux
Adding `set -e` to job.sh
Starting it in a tmux session on the server, then detaching
blocks.explain: The tmux server on the remote machine owns the shell, so losing the connection only detaches a client. With `&` alone the job stays a job of the login shell, which forwards SIGHUP. tmux on the laptop protects only the laptop side: the ssh connection and the remote shell still die. `nohup ./job.sh &` would also survive.

blocks.question: Your public key is in the server's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, yet ssh falls back to asking for a password. On the server, `ls -ld ~/.ssh` shows `drwxrwxrwx`. What is the likely cause?
options: sshd will not use authorized_keys while ~/.ssh is writable by other users
The key type is wrong for this server
known_hosts on your laptop is missing
The private key must also be copied to the server
blocks.explain: Anyone who can write to `~/.ssh` could add their own key, so sshd refuses to trust authorized_keys there (its StrictModes check). `chmod 700 ~/.ssh` and `chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys` fix it. The private key must never be copied to the server.
